Chapter 8: Advocating for Yourself — Speaking Up and Asking for What You Need.
So, once you’ve set your boundaries, what comes next? Well, it’s all about learning how to advocate for yourself. And that means speaking up for what you need, what you want, and what matters to you—even when it feels a little uncomfortable.
Let’s be honest, a lot of women are taught to be accommodating, to not “make waves,” or to wait and hope someone else recognizes their hard work. But here’s the thing: self-advocacy isn’t just helpful—it’s absolutely essential if you want to reach your personal and professional goals.
Now, advocating for yourself doesn’t mean you have to be loud or demanding. It’s really about expressing your needs clearly and confidently, and trusting that those needs are valid. Think of it like a musician tuning her instrument before she plays. She isn’t apologizing for needing the right pitch—she’s just making sure she can do her best.
Want to practice self-advocacy in your own life? Here are some gentle strategies you can try:
First, prepare ahead of time. Take a moment to figure out what you want to say, and why it matters to you.
Second, choose assertive language. Instead of saying, “I was wondering if…,” try a clear statement like, “I need…” or “I would like…”
And third, stay grounded in your values. Let what’s most important to you guide your requests and the way you respond.
For example, imagine you’re an employee hoping for a raise. You might gather evidence of your contributions, practice your main points, and walk into that conversation with calm confidence. You’re not asking for more than you deserve—you’re honoring your own value.
Remember, self-advocacy isn’t just about making requests. It’s also about knowing when to ask for help. Sometimes, it’s easy to think that being independent means never needing support. But the truth is, knowing when to reach out—that takes real wisdom, not weakness.
Over time, the more you advocate for yourself, the more your self-respect grows. And here’s a great side effect: other people start to treat you with more respect as well. With practice, self-advocacy gets easier, and it opens the door to opportunities and a deeper sense of fulfillment.
